feedback: When a learner asserts a claim, prompt them to give the evidence or mechanism behind it rather than accepting it as a rule.
For sensitive topics (weight, tobacco, alcohol), keep responses factual, focused on body systems and risk, and free of shame or moralising.
activities.intendedInsight: Health messages are evidence-based claims to reason about, not rules to obey; you can obtain information from an expert and combine it with what you know to judge a claim.
learnerActions: Ask a friendly doctor or body-systems scientist your real questions in role, e.g. 'what does smoking actually do to my lungs?'
Weigh the answer, which is grounded in mechanism and risk, and respond when gently probed ('why do you think that?').
Bring an evidence question to settle, e.g. 'what's my evidence that exercise makes the heart stronger, not just the arm and leg muscles?'
activities.title: Ask the doctor: weigh a health claim

feedback: If a learner thinks exercise only affects limb muscles, connect the raised pulse to the heart working harder as a muscle of its own.

Distinguish the two measurements: the immediate post-exercise rise shows effort now, while a resting pulse that is consistently lower after a sustained period of regular activity, measured under similar conditions, would be evidence that fits with the heart strengthening — reinforcing the cumulative idea in their own body, though some children may see little change in a few weeks.
activities.intendedInsight: Exercise works the heart itself: a pulse that rises during and after exercise shows the heart working harder, and a resting pulse that stays lower (measured carefully under similar conditions) after a sustained period of regular activity fits with the heart adapting and strengthening over time — not just a slogan, and not only about limb muscles.
learnerActions: Measure your resting heart rate, then your heart rate just after exercise, drawing on the earlier heart-rate topic.

Use the immediate difference as evidence that the heart works harder during exercise; and, over a period of regular activity, compare your resting pulse before and after that period to look for adaptation, taking several readings at the same time of day and when calm, and remembering that resting pulse also changes with things like illness, tiredness or excitement, so a small change may not show adaptation.
Explain what this shows about exercise working the heart itself, not just the arm and leg muscles.
activities.title: Connect it to your own pulse

feedback: If a learner judges health only by looking slim or feeling fine, ask what the heart, arteries, lungs or teeth are doing out of sight.

If a learner says exercise cancels smoking, separate the two: exercise strengthens the heart and breathing muscles while smoking still damages the lungs and raises heart-disease risk — one does not erase the other.
If a learner bans whole foods as 'poison', reframe around amount and frequency within an overall balance.
activities.intendedInsight: You can distinguish health from mere appearance by naming a specific internal harm, and you can read cumulative effects from data over time.
learnerActions: Match each choice to the body-system effect it causes.
Judge a given health claim as reasonable or not and say why, using mechanism and risk.
Interpret a simple data/timeline item showing how an effect builds up cumulatively over time.

Reason about transfer cases: how two people of the same weight can differ in heart health; why a frequently sugary diet raises the risk of tooth decay even without weight gain; whether a fit marathon runner's exercise cancels out their smoking.
activities.title: Consolidate: match, judge, interpret
